reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because the creator promotes signing up for Binance through a referral link, explaining that it is a cryptocurrency trading platform and showing its registration page and market listings. He urges viewers to join before he claims registration may close again, but the video does not promise viewers a return or ask them to send money or provide data to the creator. The referral promotion and urgency are observable, while the available content does not establish a deceptive solicitation.

opening.argument: The video links concrete viewer actions to digital-asset rewards. The speaker asks viewers to subscribe and says that once the channel reaches 2,000 subscribers, he will conduct a Litecoin giveaway. He separately directs viewers to return to an earlier video and leave a Litecoin address for that giveaway. That is a reward solicitation tied to subscription and submission of crypto-related information, not merely discussion of cryptocurrency. The Binance registration request adds another action-for-benefit relationship because the speaker explicitly calls the signup link a referral for himself. Taken together, viewers are encouraged to perform low-effort actions in exchange for a promised cryptocurrency benefit, while the conditions and fulfillment of the reward are not established.

opening.argument: The presentation concentrates several warning signals around an easy-action crypto offer: the title says “HURRY,” the speaker repeatedly urges immediate signup, and he says the service may shut down again soon because users will flood it. The page shown in the video also places a referral-program banner saying it pays to have friends beside multiple giveaway and prize promotions. This combination makes the requested registration look less like neutral market information and more like urgency-driven acquisition tied to rewards. The description further supplies numerous cryptocurrency and mining-related referral URLs, broadening the promotional environment beyond a single informational demonstration. Even without a stated deposit, the low-barrier action, crypto incentives, external links, and time pressure collectively support treating the offer as deceptive reward solicitation.

The visible page does not merely show trading; it prominently displays a referral-program message and prize promotions. Those signals matter when evaluating whether the video is steering viewers through a reward-oriented acquisition funnel rather than simply explaining a platform.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Urgency alone does not establish a scam: the speaker explains the claimed reason as possible service closure from user demand, then describes Binance as a trading platform. The page’s referral and giveaway banners show promotions, but they do not show that viewers were promised a guaranteed return or that a reward required payment. The description contains referral URLs, yet the available evidence does not establish that those links were deceptive or that viewers were harmed.

opening.argument: Although the speaker adopts the tone of breaking cryptocurrency news and demonstrating a trading platform, the practical function is direct user acquisition. He repeatedly tells viewers to click the description link and register, identifies the link as his referral, and promises further tutorials about depositing Bitcoin and making trades. The description reinforces that promotional role by listing many named cryptocurrency services with referral URLs. The market discussion therefore serves as a pathway into referral-driven participation, rather than standing alone as education. The displayed referral-program banner, including the message that it pays to have friends, further supports reading the video as incentive-based recruitment. A judge should evaluate the call to participate as the operative content, not let the explanatory framing obscure the commission-oriented promotion.
